Before you can require a linear commit history, your repository must allow squash merging or rebase merging. For more information, see [Configuring pull request merges](/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges).

## Require deployments to succeed before merging

You can require that changes are successfully deployed to specific environments before a branch can be merged. For example, you can use this rule to ensure that changes are successfully deployed to a staging environment before the changes merge to your default branch.

For stacked pull requests, deploying a pull request also satisfies this requirement for pull requests below it while the stack has a linear history. See [Stacked pull requests](/en/pull-requests/reference/stacked-pull-requests#branch-protections-and-required-checks).

## Require signed commits

When you enable required commit signing on a branch, contributors and bots can only push commits that have been signed and verified to the branch. For more information, see [About commit signature verification](/en/authentication/managing-commit-signature-verification/about-commit-signature-verification).

Branch protection rules and rulesets behave differently when you create a branch: with rulesets, we check only the commits that aren't accessible from other branches, whereas with branch protection rules, we do not verify signed commits unless you restrict pushes that create matching branches. With both, when you update a branch, we still check all the commits in the specified range, even if a commit is reachable from other branches.

With both methods, we use the `verified_signature?` to confirm if a commit has a valid signature. If not, the update is not accepted.

> [!NOTE]
>
> * If you have enabled vigilant mode in your account settings, which indicates that your commits will always be signed, any commits that GitHub identifies as "Partially verified" are permitted on branches that require signed commits. For more information about vigilant mode, see [Displaying verification statuses for all of your commits](/en/authentication/managing-commit-signature-verification/displaying-verification-statuses-for-all-of-your-commits).
> * If a collaborator pushes an unsigned commit to a branch that requires commit signatures, the collaborator will need to rebase the commit to include a verified signature, then force push the rewritten commit to the branch.

You can push local commits to the branch if the commits are signed and verified.

You can also merge signed and verified commits into the branch using a pull request. When GitHub evaluates whether a pull request can be merged, it creates a test merge commit whose parents are the latest commit on the base branch and the pull request's head commit. GitHub checks the commits introduced by this test merge, including commits from the head branch. As a result, unsigned commits on the head branch can block a squash merge, even though GitHub would sign the final squash commit. This restriction can also apply to the author of the pull request.

To merge a blocked pull request, rewrite and sign the unsigned commits on the head branch, or ask someone with permission to bypass the applicable protections to merge the pull request.

You can squash and merge pull requests locally, but you must sign the resulting commit before pushing it to the branch. If another protection requires changes to be made through a pull request, you may also need bypass permissions to push the locally merged commit. See [Checking out pull requests locally](/en/pull-requests/how-tos/review-pull-requests/checking-out-pull-requests-locally) and [Signing commits](/en/authentication/managing-commit-signature-verification/signing-commits).

For more information about merge methods, see [About merge methods on GitHub](/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/about-merge-methods-on-github).

## Require a pull request before merging

You can require that all changes to the target branch be associated with a pull request. The pull request doesn't necessarily have to be approved, but it must be opened.

### Additional settings

> [!NOTE] If you select **Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed** and/or **Require approval of the most recent reviewable push**, manually creating the merge commit for a pull request and pushing it directly to a protected branch will fail, unless the contents of the merge exactly match the merge generated by GitHub for the pull request.
>
> In addition, with these settings, approving reviews will be dismissed as stale if the merge base introduces new changes after the review was submitted. The merge base is the commit that is the last common ancestor between the topic branch and the base branch. If the merge base changes, the pull request cannot be merged until someone approves the work again.

Repository administrators or custom roles with the "edit repository rules" permission can require that all pull requests receive a specific number of approving reviews before someone merges the pull request into a protected branch. You can require approving reviews from people with write permissions in the repository or from a designated code owner.

If you enable required reviews, collaborators can only push changes to a branch via a pull request that is approved by the required number of reviewers with write permissions.

If someone chooses the **Request changes** option in a review, then that person must approve the pull request before the pull request can be merged. If a reviewer who requests changes on a pull request isn't available, anyone with write permissions for the repository can dismiss the blocking review.

Even after all required reviewers have approved a pull request, collaborators cannot merge the pull request if there are other open pull requests that have a head branch pointing to the same commit with pending or rejected reviews. Someone with write permissions must approve or dismiss the blocking review on the other pull requests first.

Optionally, you can choose to dismiss stale pull request approvals when commits are pushed that affect the diff in the pull request. GitHub records the state of the diff at the point when a pull request is approved. This state represents the set of changes that the reviewer approved. If the diff changes from this state (for example, because a contributor pushes new changes to the pull request branch or clicks **Update branch**, or because a related pull request is merged into the target branch), the approving review is dismissed as stale, and the pull request cannot be merged until someone app

Optionally, you can choose to require reviews from code owners. If you do, any pull request that modifies content with a code owner must be approved by that code owner before the pull request can be merged into the protected branch. Note that if code has multiple owners, an approval from *any* of the code owners will be sufficient to meet this requirement. For more information, see [About code owners](/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/about-code-owners).

Optionally, you can restrict who can dismiss pull request reviews. If you enable this setting, select the users, teams, or GitHub Apps that can dismiss reviews on branches targeted by the ruleset. You can configure this setting in the UI or through the REST API or GraphQL API. For more information, see [Dismissing a pull request review](/en/pull-requests/how-tos/review-pull-requests/dismissing-a-pull-request-review).

Optionally, you can require an approval from someone other than the last person to push to a branch before a pull request can be merged. This means at least one other authorized reviewer has approved any changes. For example, the "last reviewer" can check that the latest set of changes incorporates feedback from other reviews, and does not add new, unreviewed content.

For complex pull requests that require many reviews, requiring an approval from someone other than the last person to push can be a compromise that avoids the need to dismiss all stale reviews: with this option, "stale" reviews are not dismissed, and the pull request remains approved as long as someone other than the person who made the most recent changes approves it. Users who have already reviewed a pull request can reapprove after the most recent push to meet this requirement. If you are concerned about pull requests being "hijacked" (where unapproved content is added to approved pull requ

Optionally, you can require all comments on the pull request to be resolved before it can be merged to a branch. This ensures that all comments are addressed or acknowledged before merge.

Optionally, you can require a merge type of merge, squash, or rebase. This means the targeted branches may only be merged based on the allowed type. Additionally if the repository has disabled a merge method and the ruleset required a different method, the merge will be blocked. See [About merge methods on GitHub](/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/about-merge-methods-on-github).

#### Additional approval for unattributed Copilot pull requests

> [!NOTE]
> This feature is in public preview and subject to change.

**Require an additional approval for unattributed Copilot pull requests** is enabled by default, for both new and existing rulesets. When Copilot opens a pull request that isn't attributed to a person, the ruleset requires one more approval than the number you configured. For example, a ruleset that requires one approval requires two approvals from people with write access.

Requiring one approval usually means two people are involved in a change: the person who wrote it and the person who approved it. That assumption doesn't hold when Copilot opens a pull request under its own app identity instead of on behalf of a person, for example when you prompt it from a shared context such as a group thread or channel. See [Integrating Copilot cloud agent with Slack](/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-integrations/integrate-cloud-agent-with-slack) and [Integrating Copilot cloud agent with Teams](/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-integrations/integrate-cloud-agent-with-teams).

This setting has no effect if the ruleset requires zero approvals, so repositories that use pull requests as a record of changes rather than to gate on approvals are unaffected.

If you clear this setting, these pull requests require only the number of approvals you configured. If you also require an approval from someone other than the last person to push, at least one approval must cover the last push and come from someone other than Copilot.

#### Required reviewers

Optionally, you can require review or approval from specific teams when a pull request changes certain files or directories. You can specify up to 15 different teams, and for each team you can require a certain number of approvals from team members. For an approval from a team member to count, the team must have write permissions (or higher) for the repository.

The **Reviewer** dropdown allows you to select any team which is in scope where the rule is being defined.

* **Organization-wide rules**: The team must belong to the organization.
* **Repository-level rules**: The team must belong to the organization that owns the repository.

This rule is not available on user-owned repositories as they do not contain teams.

Required approvals can be set from 0 (zero) to 10. Requiring zero approvals means that the team will be added for visibility, but the team does not need to approve the request.

For each team, you can specify a list of file patterns which determines what files the setting applies to. The format of this file list is the same as a standard [`.gitignore`](/en/get-started/git-basics/ignoring-files) file:

* A pattern starting with an exclamation mark (`!`) is a negation. This will cause paths matching earlier patterns to *not* require approvals.
* Patterns are matched in order, so negated patterns can "unmatch" files which matched previous rules.

## Require status checks to pass before merging

Required status checks ensure that all required CI tests are passing before collaborators can make changes to a branch or tag targeted by your ruleset. Required status checks can be checks or statuses. For more information, see [Status checks](/en/pull-requests/reference/status-checks).

You can use the commit status API to allow external services to mark commits with an appropriate status. For more information, see [REST API endpoints for commit statuses](/en/rest/commits/statuses).

After enabling required status checks, all required status checks must pass before collaborators can merge changes into the branch or tag.

Any person or integration with write permissions to a repository can set the state of any status check in the repository, but in some cases you may only want to accept a status check from a specific GitHub App. When you add a required status check rule, you can select an app as the expected source of status updates. The app must be installed in the repository with the `statuses:write` permission, must have recently submitted a check run, and must be associated with a pre-existing required status check in the ruleset. If the status is set by any other person or integration, merging won't be all

To troubleshoot issues with configuring status checks in rulesets, see [Troubleshooting rules](/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/troubleshooting-rules#troubleshooting-required-status-checks).

You can think of required status checks as being either "loose" or "strict." The type of required status check you choose determines whether your branch is required to be up to date with the base branch before merging.
* Code Quality found a result of a severity of the level defined in the ruleset, or a higher severity.

For more information, see [GitHub Code Quality](/en/code-security/concepts/code-quality/code-quality) and [Setting code quality thresholds for pull requests](/en/code-security/how-tos/maintain-quality-code/set-pr-thresholds).

## Require license compliance results before merging

This enables the license compliance feature on the targeted repositories. License compliance checks added or changed dependencies against a policy of permitted licenses and will block pull requests which add dependencies whose licenses are not allowed. For more information, see [About open source license compliance](/en/code-security/concepts/supply-chain-security/open-source-license-compliance).

## Restrict code coverage

> [!NOTE]
> This feature is in public preview and subject to change.

If your repository has GitHub Code Quality enabled and code coverage data is being uploaded, you can use rulesets to prevent pull requests from being merged based on code coverage thresholds. For more information about uploading coverage data, see [Setting up code coverage for your repository](/en/code-security/how-tos/maintain-quality-code/set-up-code-coverage).

The rule evaluates only coverage data that has already been uploaded and does not wait for coverage uploads to complete. To ensure that all expected coverage results are evaluated before a pull request can be merged, make each status check associated with an expected coverage upload a required status check.

This rule blocks a pull request from being merged when either of two code coverage thresholds is not met:

* **Minimum line coverage percentage**: the aggregated line coverage for the pull request branch is below the configured percentage.
* **Maximum line coverage drop**: line coverage drops by more than the configured number of percentage points relative to the default branch.

For how to configure the thresholds, the prerequisite for uploading coverage data, and how to roll the rule out safely, see [Setting code coverage thresholds for pull requests](/en/code-security/how-tos/maintain-quality-code/restrict-code-coverage).

## Restrict file paths

Prevent commits that include changes in specified file paths from being pushed to the repository. Limit is 200 entries and up to 200 characters in each entry.

You can use `fnmatch` syntax for this. For example, a restriction targeting `test/demo/**/*` prevents any pushes to files or folders in the `test/demo/` directory. A restriction targeting `test/docs/pushrules.md` prevents pushes specifically to the `pushrules.md` file in the `test/docs/` directory. For more information, see [Creating rulesets for a repository](/en/repositories/configuring-branches

You can also add allowed exceptions to this rule. A file matching an allowed exception can be pushed even when it also matches a restricted path.

## Overview

OpenID Connect (OIDC) allows your GitHub Actions workflows to access resources in Amazon Web Services (AWS), without needing to store the AWS credentials as long-lived GitHub secrets.

This guide explains how to configure AWS to trust GitHub's OIDC as a federated identity, and includes a workflow example for the [`aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials`](https://github.com/aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials) that uses tokens to authenticate to AWS and access resources.

> [!NOTE]
> Support for custom claims for OIDC is unavailable in AWS.

## Prerequisites

# Using OpenID Connect with reusable workflows
You can use reusable workflows with OIDC to standardize and security harden your deployment steps.
## About reusable workflows
Rather than copying and pasting deployment jobs from one workflow to another, you can create a reusable workflow that performs the deployment steps. A reusable workflow can be used by another workflow if it meets one of the access requirements described in [Reusing workflow configurations](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/reusing-workflow-configurations#access-to-reusable-workflows).
You should be familiar with the concepts described in [Reuse workflows](/en/actions/how-tos/reuse-automations/reuse-workflows) and [OpenID Connect reference](/en/actions/reference/security/oidc#customizing-the-token-claims).
## Defining the trust conditions
When combined with OpenID Connect (OIDC), reusable workflows let you enforce consistent deployments across your repository, organization, or enterprise. You can do this by defining trust conditions on cloud roles based on reusable workflows. The available options will vary depending on your cloud provider:
* **Using `job_workflow_ref`:**
  * To create trust conditions based on reusable workflows, your cloud provider must support custom claims for `job_workflow_ref`. This allows your cloud provider to identify which repository the job originally came from.
  * For clouds that only support the standard claims (audience (`aud`) and subject (`sub`)), you can use the API to customize the `sub` claim to include `job_workflow_ref`. For more information, see [OpenID Connect reference](/en/actions/reference/security/oidc#customizing-the-token-claims). Support for custom claims is currently available for Google Cloud Platform and HashiCorp Vault.
* **Customizing the token claims:**
  * You can configure more granular trust conditions by customizing the subject (`sub`) claim that's included with the JWT. For more information, see [OpenID Connect](/en/actions/concepts/security/openid-connect).
## How the token works with reusable workflows
During a workflow run, GitHub's OIDC provider presents an OIDC token to the cloud provider which contains information about the job. If that job is part of a reusable workflow, the token will include the standard claims that contain information about the calling workflow, and will also include a custom claim called `job_workflow_ref` that contains information about the called workflow.
For example, the following OIDC token is for a job that was part of a called workflow. The `workflow`, `ref`, and other attributes describe the caller workflow, while `job_workflow_ref` refers to the called workflow:
```yaml copy
{
  "typ": "JWT",
  "alg": "RS256",
  "x5t": "example-thumbprint",
  "kid": "example-key-id"
}
{
  "jti": "example-id",
  "sub": "repo:octo-org/octo-repo:environment:prod",
  "aud": "https://github.com/octo-org",
  "ref": "refs/heads/main",
  "sha": "example-sha",
  "repository": "octo-org/octo-repo",
  "repository_owner": "octo-org",
  "actor_id": "12",
  "repository_id": "74",
  "repository_owner_id": "65",
  "run_id": "example-run-id",
  "run_number": "10",
  "run_attempt": "2",
  "actor": "octocat",
  "workflow": "example-workflow",
  "head_ref": "",

Đây là review độc lập Topic 3 (3.1–3.7) trong `/home/do.hoang.minh.hung/papaya-devsecops-challenge/work/02-research.md`. Tôi không sửa file nào.

**Đã kiểm tra:** từng trích dẫn đều được so với bản copy trong `scratchpad/docs/gh/`. Banner gói (plan) lấy từ field `"product"` trong file HTML. Tôi tải thêm vào `/tmp/claude-1001/-home-do-hoang-minh-hung-papaya-devsecops-challenge/2e770088-3c42-4cef-b063-5c554b20a853/scratchpad/rev3/` các trang: `creating-rulesets-for-a-repository`, `oidc-with-reusable-workflows`, `managing-a-merge-queue` và trang Google `workload-identity-federation-with-deployment-pipelines`. Tất cả 19 link docs.github.com trong Topic 3 trả HTTP 200 qua API.

**Các điểm đúng (✅ đã đối chiếu):**
- 3.1.2 đúng nguyên văn. `deployments-and-environments` ghi: "If you are on a GitHub Free, GitHub Pro, or GitHub Team plan, required reviewers are only available for public repositories". Câu tương tự có cho wait timers, admin bypass và custom rules. Deployment branches/tags thì "also available for private repositories" với Pro/Team.
- Banner rulesets / push rulesets / protected branches / code owners khớp nguyên văn. Như vậy rulesets, path-based required reviewers và push rulesets đều có trên Team private.
- Các con số đều đúng: 6 reviewers, tối đa 6 rules mỗi environment, 75 rulesets, 15 teams, 0–10 approvals, 200 entries, 3 MB, 180 ngày, 6 giờ, mốc July 15, 2026.

## Findings

**HIGH-1 — 3.6 #1 và #2 (dựa trên 3.1.3, 3.4.3): "chỉ code đã merge và đã duyệt mới lấy được prod credentials" là kết luận quá mức.**
- Rule deployment-branch so với `GITHUB_REF` (3.1.3). Nhưng với `issue_comment`, `workflow_run` và `schedule`, `GITHUB_REF` = "Default branch" (bảng trong `events-that-trigger-workflows`). `pull_request_target` "runs in the context of the default branch".
- Hệ quả: mọi workflow file trên `main` có tham chiếu `environment: production` đều qua được rule "chỉ main", bất kể trigger là gì. Ví dụ: workflow `claude-code-action` chạy theo `issue_comment`, hoặc một workflow `pull_request_target` checkout code của PR.
- `sub` dạng environment cũng không chứa event hay workflow, nên AWS không phân biệt được các trường hợp này.
- `workflow_dispatch` thì lấy `GITHUB_REF` = "Branch or tag that received dispatch". Nên dispatch từ nhánh khác main **bị** chặn (trả lời câu hỏi trong scope). Nhưng nếu dispatch trên `main` mà workflow nhận input ref/sha rồi checkout ref đó, thì vẫn deploy được code chưa merge.
- **Sửa:** ghi điều kiện này vào 3.6 #1/#2. Các cách khắc phục:
  - Giới hạn workflow nào được tham chiếu `production`: CODEOWNERS trên `.github/workflows` cộng với một CI check.
  - Customise `sub` để thêm `job_workflow_ref`, và/hoặc thêm claim về workflow/event (⚠️ cần xác nhận claim nào được đưa vào `include_claim_keys`).
  - Deploy workflow không nhận input ref.
  - Không có job `production` nào chạy theo trigger privileged.

**MEDIUM-1 — 3.3.4 (bullet "required status check"): thiếu điều kiện chống giả mạo.**
- `available-rules-for-rulesets` ghi: "Any person or integration with write permissions to a repository can set the state of any status check… you can select an app as the expected source of status updates."
- Nếu không pin nguồn bằng app, chính job agent có `statuses: write` có thể tự đặt check thành pass.
- **Sửa:** ghi rõ là phải chọn expected source app.

**MEDIUM-2 — 3.6 #1 ("no bypass"): thiếu phần quyền admin.**
- Ruleset không có bypass mặc định. `creating-rulesets-for-a-repository` cho thấy bypass list phải tự thêm, gồm "Repository admins, organization owners…". Đây là điểm khác với branch protection (3.2.6), nên ghi ra.
- Repo admin và người có quyền "edit repository rules" có thể sửa hoặc tắt ruleset và environment. Việc này có log (`repository_ruleset.update`, `environment.update_protection_rule`), nhưng không bị chặn.
- Repo admin cũng có thể reset OIDC `sub` customization ("a repository administrator must use the REST API… `use_default`", trang `oidc`).
- **Sửa:** thêm vào 3.6: số người giữ quyền admin/owner phải ít và có review định kỳ; cảnh báo theo các audit event trên.

**MEDIUM-3 — 3.4.x: thiếu phía GCP.**
- Trang Google (đã đọc): "To help protect against spoofing threats, you must use an attribute condition that restricts access to tokens issued by your GitHub organization." Yêu cầu này chặt hơn câu "at least one condition" của GitHub.
- `oidc-with-reusable-workflows` ghi: "Support for custom claims is currently available for Google Cloud Platform". Nghĩa là trên GCP có thể đặt điều kiện trực tiếp trên `job_workflow_ref`, `ref`, `event_name`. Trên AWS thì không, phải qua `sub`.
- **Sửa:** thêm một dòng cho GCP. Sửa 3.6 #2 để không nói kiểu chỉ có AWS.

**LOW-1 — 3.4.5:** câu "a customised `sub` still works with AWS's `:sub` condition" là suy luận nhưng đang gắn ✅, và hai trang được trích không nói điều này. Trang `oidc-with-reusable-workflows` có nói: "For clouds that only support the standard claims (`aud` and `sub`), you can use the API to customize the `sub` claim to include `job_workflow_ref`." **Sửa:** cite trang này, hoặc đổi marker sang ⚠️.

**LOW-2 — 3.4.2:** câu về Dependabot bị mất điều kiện. Nguồn ghi "…**and your cloud provider supports conditions on `event_name`**, allow only…". AWS không hỗ trợ custom claims. **Sửa:** giữ nguyên điều kiện, và ghi rằng trên AWS chỉ làm được qua `sub` customization.

**LOW-3 — 3.4.3, phần inference:** "not by AWS" chỉ đúng với `sub` mặc định. **Sửa:** thêm "with the default `sub` format" (cách khắc phục: xem MEDIUM-3 và LOW-1).

**LOW-4 — 3.5.1 và 3.6 #4:**
- Câu "agent step can rewrite… / not tamper-proof" là suy luận nhưng nằm trong dòng ✅. Nó còn phụ thuộc vào việc tool config của agent có cho chạy shell/`sudo` hay không.
- Runner single-CPU (`ubuntu-slim`) là "hosted in a container on a shared VM", và trang không nói nó có sudo hay không.
- **Sửa:** gắn nhãn inference cho câu này, và giới hạn câu "agent has root" vào trường hợp agent có quyền Bash không hạn chế.

**LOW-5 — 3.2.1:** cùng trang `about-rulesets`, dòng 7 viết: "applies to a repository or to multiple repositories in an organization for customers on GitHub Team and GitHub Enterprise plans". Dòng 11 lại viết org-level chỉ có trên Enterprise. **Sửa:** ghi lại sự mâu thuẫn và giữ ⚠️ cho câu hỏi org-level trên Team. Có thể thêm con số "75 organization-wide rulesets".

**LOW-6 — 3.1.4 và 3.7:** trên Team private, bảo vệ duy nhất của environment là branch restriction. Câu hỏi thực sự là admin có bypass hay sửa được branch restriction hay không, chứ không phải "default admin-bypass". **Sửa:** đổi lại câu hỏi mở.

**LOW-7 — 3.3.1:** trích dẫn bị cắt. Nguyên văn: "…if it was you who assigned Copilot **to the issue to which the pull request relates**". Cũng nên thêm: "Approvals by GitHub Copilot… do not count toward those requirements."

**LOW-8 — 3.3.3:** chỉ trích event cấp org. Event cấp repo `repo.set_workflow_permission_can_approve_pr` cũng có trong `audit-log-events`. Nên thêm.

**LOW-9 — 3.3.4 và 3.2.4:**
- Câu "the author is the app" được nói như sự thật, trong khi nó phụ thuộc vào cách `claude-code-action` tạo PR (open item 3.7). **Sửa:** viết thành câu điều kiện ("if the app opens the PR…").
- Câu "This works in a monorepo: e.g. `infra/**` 2 approvals" là suy luận chưa gắn nhãn.

**LOW-10 — 3.5.6 và 3.6 #6:** trang đã đọc (`reviewing-the-audit-log…`, mục "Exporting the audit log") có ghi export JSON/CSV kèm "Export limits". Nên ghi đây là lựa chọn ✅. Streaming vẫn giữ ⚠️.

## Coverage gaps
1. Chưa rõ approval từ GitHub App (vd. Claude app có `pull_requests: write`) có được tính vào số approval bắt buộc không. Copilot thì không được tính. Ghi ⚠️ và thêm vào 3.7.
2. Repo secrets: `secure-use` ghi "Any user with write access to your repository has read access to all secrets configured in your repository". Vì vậy prod creds chỉ được nằm trong environment hoặc qua OIDC. Nên thêm vào 3.6.

- Rule deployment-branch so với `GITHUB_REF` (3.1.3). Nhưng với `issue_comment`, `workflow_run` và `schedule`, `GITHUB_REF` = "Default branch" (bảng trong `events-that-trigger-workflows`). `pull_request_target` "runs in the context of the default branch".
- Hệ quả: mọi workflow file trên `main` có tham chiếu `environment: production` đều qua được rule "chỉ main", bất kể trigger là gì. Ví dụ: workflow `claude-code-action` chạy theo `issue_comment`, hoặc một workflow `pull_request_target` checkout code của PR.
- `sub` dạng environment cũng không chứa event hay workflow, nên AWS không phân biệt được các trường hợp này.
- `workflow_dispatch` thì lấy `GITHUB_REF` = "Branch or tag that received dispatch". Nên dispatch từ nhánh khác main **bị** chặn (trả lời câu hỏi trong scope). Nhưng nếu dispatch trên `main` mà workflow nhận input ref/sha rồi checkout ref đó, thì vẫn deploy được code chưa merge.
- **Sửa:** ghi điều kiện này vào 3.6 #1/#2. Các cách khắc phục:

130	### 3.6 What this means for Papaya (inferences — to be used in the design)
131	
132	These are my conclusions from the findings above, not documented facts:
133	
134	1. **The GitHub plan decides where the "named human approved it" gate can sit.**
135	   - **On Enterprise Cloud:** a `production` environment with required reviewers, prevent
136	     self-review, no admin bypass, and deployment branches = `main` (3.1.1–3.1.4). The approval
137	     is per deployment job and logged as `workflows.approve_workflow_job` (3.5.6).
138	   - **On Team:** environments have **no approval gate** on a private repo (3.1.2). The gate must
139	     be the **PR merge to `main`**, enforced by:
140	     - rulesets: PR required, ≥1–2 approvals, code-owner review, path-based team reviewers for
141	       `infra/**` and `.github/**`, dismiss stale approvals, last-push approval, an empty bypass
142	       list (3.2.2–3.2.4);
143	     - the `production` environment restricted to `main` (3.1.3).
144	   - **Prerequisite on both plans: the branch rule alone does not mean "only merged, approved
145	     code reaches prod".** Every workflow on `main` passes a "main only" rule, whatever its trigger
146	     (3.4.5c). So all of the following must also hold:
147	     - only reviewed deploy workflows may reference `production`, enforced by CODEOWNERS on
148	       `.github/workflows` and a CI check;
149	     - deploy workflows take no ref or SHA input, and deploy the commit they run on;
150	     - no `production` job runs on `issue_comment`, `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run`;
151	     - preferably, the `sub` claim is pinned to the reusable deploy workflow (`job_workflow_ref`,
152	       3.4.5).
153	
154	     Under these conditions, merge approval equals deploy approval on Team.
155	   - **Admins remain a gap.** Admins and holders of "edit repository rules" can edit rulesets,
156	     environments and the OIDC `sub` customisation. This is logged, not prevented (3.1.4, 3.2.2,
157	     3.4.5). So: few admins, periodic access review, and alerts on `repository_ruleset.update`,
158	     `environment.update_protection_rule` and `protected_branch.policy_override`.
159	   - **GĐ-5 holds only on Enterprise.** It should go back to the framing as a correction and an
160	     open question for Papaya.
161	2. **OIDC trust must pin the repository, the gate and, where possible, the workflow** (3.4.2–3.4.5c):
162	   - **AWS:** prod roles trust only `repo:<org>/<repo>:environment:production`, in the repo's
163	     `sub` format (3.4.4). Ideally a customised `sub` includes `job_workflow_ref`, because AWS
164	     cannot test other claims (3.4.5).
165	   - **GCP:** the attribute condition must restrict to the GitHub organization (required by
166	     Google). It can also test `job_workflow_ref`, `ref` and `event_name` directly (3.4.5b).
167	   - **Non-prod:** roles trust a separate environment.
168	   - **Secrets:** prod credentials never live in repository secrets, because anyone with write
169	     access can read those (3.5.6). This removes the long-lived AWS keys from the brief (P5).
170	3. **Agent-authored PRs need one more rule than human PRs** (3.3.4). Opening PRs with the
171	   engineer's own identity keeps GitHub's built-in author rule. App-authored PRs need 2 approvals
172	   or a custom check whose source app is pinned. "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull
173	   requests" stays **off** (3.3.3).
174	4. **CI agents and policy files:** on standard GitHub-hosted runners, an agent with shell access
175	   has root, so Claude Code managed settings written in the job are advisory (3.5.1, closes the
176	   Topic 1 question). The real limits for a CI agent are:
177	   - the job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions (3.5.3);
178	   - **no** `environment: production` in any agent workflow, so it gets no prod OIDC trust
179	     (3.4.5c);
180	   - the base-branch config restore in `claude-code-action` (1.7.9).
181	
182	   Self-hosted runners would allow a root-owned policy, but bring persistence risks (3.5.2).
183	5. **Supply chain of CI itself:**
184	   - Workflow lockfile or SHA pinning, enforced by org policy (3.5.5).
185	   - CODEOWNERS on `.github/` (3.2.8), plus CI validation of the CODEOWNERS file, because invalid
186	     lines fail silently (3.2.7).
187	   - Restricted default `GITHUB_TOKEN` (3.5.3); no `pull_request_target` with checkout (3.5.4).
188	6. **Audit retention gap:** the org audit log keeps 180 days (3.5.6). ISO 27001 and HIPAA evidence
189	   needs longer, so it must be exported periodically (JSON or CSV, within the export limits, ✅)
190	   or streamed (⚠️ not researched; may be Enterprise-only).
191	
192	### 3.7 Open items (Topic 3)
193	
194	- [ ] ⚠️ **Papaya's GitHub plan** (Team vs Enterprise Cloud). It decides 3.6 #1 and corrects GĐ-5.
195	- [ ] ⚠️ On Team private repos, can admins bypass or simply edit the environment branch
196	      restriction (3.1.4)? Are org-level rulesets available on Team (3.2.1, the docs contradict
197	      each other)?
198	- [ ] ⚠️ Which plans allow OIDC subject customisation (3.4.5), and whether Papaya's monorepo uses
199	      the old or the immutable `sub` format (3.4.4).
200	- [ ] ⚠️ Audit-log streaming and its plan; meaning of `actor_is_agent` (3.5.6).
201	- [ ] ⚠️ How the Claude GitHub App attributes PRs and commits, whether the triggering human is
202	      recorded anywhere usable for a self-approval check, and whether an approval from a GitHub
203	      App counts toward required approvals (Copilot's does not, 3.3.1) (3.3.4).
204	- [ ] ⚠️ Does Papaya use a merge queue? (`merge_group` runs carry the merge-group ref, 3.4.5c.)
205	- [ ] ⚠️ Does sudo exist on single-CPU hosted runners (3.5.1)?

## Lỗi mới hoặc còn sót

**NEW-M1 (MEDIUM) — 3.1.4 và 3.6 #1, câu "logged as `environment.update_protection_rule`": nói quá điều nguồn ghi.**
- Trang `audit-log-events` mô tả event này là "A GitHub Actions deployment protection rule was updated **via the API**". Các field của nó là `approvers`, `can_admins_bypass`, `prevent_self_review`.
- Trong các trang đã đọc không có event nào cho việc sửa deployment-branch policy. Trên Team private, đây lại là bảo vệ duy nhất của environment.
- Nguồn có event `environment.delete` ("An environment was deleted"). Đồng thời `manage-environments` ghi: "Running a workflow that references an environment that does not exist will create an environment with the referenced name."
- Suy luận (⚠️): nếu một admin xoá `production`, workflow kế tiếp tham chiếu nó sẽ tạo lại một environment không có bảo vệ. `sub` vẫn là `environment:production`, nên AWS trust vẫn chấp nhận.
- **Sửa:**
  - Thêm qualifier "via the API".
  - Ghi ⚠️ là chưa tìm thấy event được document cho thay đổi branch policy hoặc thay đổi qua UI.
  - Thêm `environment.delete` (và `environment.remove_protection_rule`) vào danh sách alert ở 3.6 #1.
  - Thêm tình huống tạo lại environment sau khi bị xoá.

**NEW-L1 (LOW) — 3.1.4 tự mâu thuẫn, và 3.2.2 cite sai nguồn.**
- 3.1.4 ghi "Whether repository admins can… simply edit that restriction is not stated (⚠️)". Câu sau lại khẳng định "Admins can in any case change environment settings". Thực ra `manage-environments` có nói rõ: "To configure an environment in an organization repository, you must have `admin` access." Nên trích câu này và bỏ phần "edit" khỏi ⚠️. Mục mở 3.7 #2 cũng cần thu hẹp tương ứng.
- 3.2.2 trích "Repository admins, organization owners". Câu này nằm ở trang `creating-rulesets-for-a-repository`, nhưng trang này không được cite (chỉ cite `about-rulesets`). Câu "can still edit or disable … not prevented" cũng chưa có nguồn trực tiếp. `about-rulesets` chỉ có enforcement status "Disabled"; câu "edit repository rules" nằm ở `available-rules-for-rulesets`.
- **Sửa:** thêm link https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/creating-rulesets-for-a-repository, và gắn nhãn inference cho phần "not prevented".
- `repository_ruleset.update` = "A repository ruleset was edited": đúng.

**NEW-L2 (LOW) — 3.4.5b, câu "So on GCP, conditions can test `job_workflow_ref`, `ref` or `event_name` directly".**
- Đây là suy luận từ "custom claims are supported" và từ cơ chế attribute mapping. Không trang nào đã đọc nói đúng như vậy.
- **Sửa:** ghi "Inference:" hoặc ⚠️ cho câu này.

**NEW-L3 (LOW) — 3.5.6: bullet "Secrets" đặt sai chỗ.**
- Câu quote về repository secrets nằm trong dòng audit log, và 3.6 #2 cite 3.5.6 cho nội dung này.
- **Sửa:** chuyển sang 3.5.3 hoặc 3.5.5, hoặc tạo dòng riêng. Đây chỉ là sửa cấu trúc; quote đã đúng.

**NEW-L4 (LOW) — 3.6 #1, danh sách trigger bị cấm.**
- Danh sách có `issue_comment`, `pull_request_target`, `workflow_run` nhưng thiếu `schedule`, dù 3.4.5c có nêu `schedule`.
- **Sửa:** thêm `schedule`, hoặc ghi lý do được phép (deploy định kỳ của commit hiện tại trên main thì có thể chấp nhận).

**Đếm:** FIXED 13, PARTLY 1, NOT FIXED 0. Lỗi mới: HIGH 0 · MEDIUM 1 · LOW 4.

content.content:
704:| 3.1.4 | "By default, administrators can bypass the protection rules and force deployments". An environment can be configured to disallow this. A bypass is possible only while a job is "Pending". On Team private repos the setting is unavailable, and the branch restriction is the only environment protection. "To configure an environment in an organization repository, you must have `admin` access", so admins can change it. Whether they can also *bypass* it at run time is not stated (⚠️).
726:| 3.2.2 | Rulesets layer: "if multiple rulesets target the same branch … the most restrictive version of the rule applies", and they also layer with branch protection rules. "Anyone with read access to a repository can view its active rulesets", including auditors. Bypass can be granted to roles, teams or GitHub Apps. The bypass list is opt-in: eligible entries such as "Repository admins, organization owners" must be added. This differs from branch protection, which exempts admins by default (3.2.6). A ruleset can be set to "Disabled", and admins or custom roles with "edit repository rules" manage rules. Inference (⚠️): those people can therefore edit or disable a ruleset, and nothing in the pages read prevents it. Edits are logged as `repository_ruleset.update` ("A repository ruleset was edited"). | ✅ / ⚠️ (inference) | [about-rulesets](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/about-rulesets), [creating-rulesets-for-a-repository](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/creating-rulesets-for-a-repository), [available-rules-for-rulesets](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/available-rules-for-rulesets) |
805:| 3.5.3b | **Repository secrets:** "Any user with write access to your repository has read access to all secrets configured in your repository". | ✅ | [secure-use](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use) |
| 3.4.5b | **GCP side:**
- Google requires more than GitHub's "at least one condition": "To help protect against spoofing threats, you must use an attribute condition that restricts access to tokens issued by your GitHub organization".
- GitHub: "Support for custom claims is currently available for Google Cloud Platform and HashiCorp Vault". Inference (⚠️): so on GCP, attribute conditions can test `job_workflow_ref`, `ref` or `event_name` directly, without customising `sub`. No page read says this in so many words.
- In a token from a reusable workflow, `ref` and `workflow` describe the **caller**, and `job_workflow_ref` describes the **called** workflow.
- `principalSet` direct access, without a service account, and conditions on immutable IDs were not read in detail (📖).

| ✅ / 📖 | [Google Cloud: workload-identity-federation-with-deployment-pipelines](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workload-identity-federation-with-deployment-pipelines), [oidc-with-reusable-workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/security-harden-deployments/oidc-with-reusable-workflows) |
| 3.4.5c | **`GITHUB_REF` per trigger**, which is what the environment branch rule matches (3.1.3):
### 3.6 What this means for Papaya (inferences — to be used in the design)

These are my conclusions from the findings above, not documented facts:

1. **The GitHub plan decides where the "named human approved it" gate can sit.**
   - **On Enterprise Cloud:** a `production` environment with required reviewers, prevent
     self-review, no admin bypass, and deployment branches = `main` (3.1.1–3.1.4). The approval
     is per deployment job and logged as `workflows.approve_workflow_job` (3.5.6).
   - **On Team:** environments have **no approval gate** on a private repo (3.1.2). The gate must
     be the **PR merge to `main`**, enforced by:
     - rulesets: PR required, ≥1–2 approvals, code-owner review, path-based team reviewers for
       `infra/**` and `.github/**`, dismiss stale approvals, last-push approval, an empty bypass
       list (3.2.2–3.2.4);
     - the `production` environment restricted to `main` (3.1.3).
   - **Prerequisite on both plans: the branch rule alone does not mean "only merged, approved
     code reaches prod".** Every workflow on `main` passes a "main only" rule, whatever its trigger
     (3.4.5c). So all of the following must also hold:
     - only reviewed deploy workflows may reference `production`, enforced by CODEOWNERS on
       `.github/workflows` and a CI check;
     - deploy workflows take no ref or SHA input, and deploy the commit they run on;
     - no `production` job runs on `issue_comment`, `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run`.
       A `schedule` deploy of the current `main` commit is acceptable only if it deploys that
       commit and takes no input;
     - preferably, the `sub` claim is pinned to the reusable deploy workflow (`job_workflow_ref`,
       3.4.5).

     Under these conditions, merge approval equals deploy approval on Team.
   - **Admins remain a gap.** Admins and holders of "edit repository rules" can edit rulesets,
     environments and the OIDC `sub` customisation. This is logged, not prevented (3.1.4, 3.2.2,
     3.4.5). So: few admins, periodic access review, and alerts on `repository_ruleset.update`,
     `environment.update_protection_rule`, `environment.remove_protection_rule`,
     `environment.delete` and `protected_branch.policy_override`.
   - **UI changes to the branch policy may not be audited** (⚠️, 3.1.4). A deleted
     `production` environment is silently recreated without protection. So a scheduled job
     should also compare the live environment configuration with the expected one, using the
     REST API, as drift detection.
   - **GĐ-5 holds only on Enterprise.** It should go back to the framing as a correction and an
     open question for Papaya.
2. **OIDC trust must pin the repository, the gate and, where possible, the workflow** (3.4.2–3.4.5c):
   - **AWS:** prod roles trust only `repo:<org>/<repo>:environment:production`, in the repo's
     `sub` format (3.4.4). Ideally a customised `sub` includes `job_workflow_ref`, because AWS
     cannot test other claims (3.4.5).
   - **GCP:** the attribute condition must restrict to the GitHub organization (required by
     Google). It can also test `job_workflow_ref`, `ref` and `event_name` directly (3.4.5b).
   - **Non-prod:** roles trust a separate environment.
   - **Secrets:** prod credentials never live in repository secrets, because anyone with write
     access can read those (3.5.3b). This removes the long-lived AWS keys from the brief (P5).
3. **Agent-authored PRs need one more rule than human PRs** (3.3.4). Opening PRs with the
   engineer's own identity keeps GitHub's built-in author rule. App-authored PRs need 2 approvals
   or a custom check whose source app is pinned. "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull
   requests" stays **off** (3.3.3).
4. **CI agents and policy files:** on standard GitHub-hosted runners, an agent with shell access
   has root, so Claude Code managed settings written in the job are advisory (3.5.1, closes the
   Topic 1 question). The real limits for a CI agent are:
   - the job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions (3.5.3);
   - **no** `environment: production` in any agent workflow, so it gets no prod OIDC trust
     (3.4.5c);
   - the base-branch config restore in `claude-code-action` (1.7.9).

   Self-hosted runners would allow a root-owned policy, but bring persistence risks (3.5.2).
5. **Supply chain of CI itself:**
   - Workflow lockfile or SHA pinning, enforced by org policy (3.5.5).
   - CODEOWNERS on `.github/` (3.2.8), plus CI validation of the CODEOWNERS file, because invalid
     lines fail silently (3.2.7).
   - Restricted default `GITHUB_TOKEN` (3.5.3); no `pull_request_target` with checkout (3.5.4).
6. **Audit retention gap:** the org audit log keeps 180 days (3.5.6). ISO 27001 and HIPAA evidence
   needs longer, so it must be exported periodically (JSON or CSV, within the export limits, ✅)
   or streamed (⚠️ not researched; may be Enterprise-only).

| 3.1.4 | "By default, administrators can bypass the protection rules and force deployments". An environment can be configured to disallow this. A bypass is possible only while a job is "Pending". On Team private repos the setting is unavailable, and the branch restriction is the only environment protection. "To configure an environment in an organization repository, you must have `admin` access", so admins can change it. Whether they can also *bypass* it at run time is not stated (⚠️).

**Audit coverage of environment changes:**
- `environment.update_protection_rule` is described as "A GitHub Actions deployment protection rule was updated **via the API**".
- No event was found in the pages read for changes to the deployment-branch policy, or for changes made in the UI (⚠️).
- `environment.delete` and `environment.remove_protection_rule` exist.
- "Running a workflow that references an environment that does not exist will create an environment with the referenced name." **Inference (⚠️):** if `production` is deleted, the next workflow that references it recreates it **without protection**. The OIDC `sub` is still `environment:production`, so the AWS trust still accepts it.

| ✅ / ⚠️ (run-time bypass, missing events, recreation) | [deployments-and-environments](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/deployments-and-environments), [review-deployments](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/deploy/configure-and-manage-deployments/review-deployments), [manage-environments](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/deploy/configure-and-manage-deployments/manage-environments), [audit-log-events](https://docs.github.com/en/organizations/keeping-your-organization-secure/managing-security-settings-for-your-organization/audit-log-events-for-your-organization) |
